result:
The premise isn't right: more agents don't always give better results. Neither five nor ten is a good starting number.

It's tempting because splitting a big program into many small functions usually helps. An agent is different from a function. Each one is a separate model loop with its own context window, so every extra agent adds costs:

- **Tokens.** Each agent re-reads its own instructions and whatever context it's handed, and you pay for that every request.
- **Handoffs.** Agents pass text to each other, and details get lost or garbled in the passing, like a game of telephone.
- **Debugging.** When an answer is wrong, you have to work out which of ten agents caused it.

Take a request like "Can I use the laser cutter Friday at 3? Book it if so." One agent with three tools (search manuals, check calendar, book) handles it in a single loop. Ten agents would add a "router", a "calendar checker", a "booking confirmer" and so on, and each would cost another model call for no gain. With a small budget, that matters.

Splitting pays off when the work is truly separable, for example:

- A single agent's context gets overloaded by too many tools or too much material.
- Independent subtasks can run in parallel.
- One part needs different instructions or permissions than the rest.

A sensible plan is to start with one agent, and make the fixed steps plain workflow code. Split only when you can name the specific problem a split would fix.

So here's a question for you. Which of the three assistant jobs (manual questions, calendar check, booking) would you test first as a candidate to split off, and what problem would the split solve?
